title: Alien megastructures or ultra-cold stars? New study maps how to spot a Dyson swarm
summary: What if some of the coldest objects in our galaxy aren't stars at all, but colossal alien power plants? A new study by Amirnezam Amiri at the University of Arkansas, soon to be published in Universe, offers a detailed blueprint for how astronomers might finally detect Dyson spheres—or more accurately, Dyson swarms. First proposed by physicist Freeman Dyson in 1960, a Dyson sphere is a hypothetical megastructure built by an advanced civilization to capture a star's energy. Modern thinking favors a "swarm" of countless orbiting solar collectors rather than a solid shell. Amiri's research tackles a crucial question: if such a structure existed, what would telescopes actually see? The answer is startling. A Dyson swarm would radically alter a star's appearance on the Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram, which plots stars by temperature and luminosity. The swarm would absorb almost all visible light, use the energy, and re-emit it as infrared heat. The total energy output—bolometric luminosity—stays the same, but the effective temperature plummets. For a typical red dwarf with a surface temperature around 3000 K, a surrounding Dyson swarm could drop the observed temperature to a frigid 50 K. No known natural object occupies that region of the H-R diagram. "Any object found there would immediately become an intriguing candidate," the study notes. Red dwarfs and white dwarfs are prime targets. Red dwarfs are the most common stars, and their small size means a Dyson swarm could orbit at just 0.05–0.3 AU, requiring far less construction material. White dwarfs offer steady energy for billions of years. The James Webb Space Telescope, with its infrared capabilities, is ideally suited for this search. In 2024, Project Hephaistos sifted through 5 million stars and flagged seven candidates, all red dwarfs. One was debunked as a background black hole, but five remain unexplained. Amiri's work adds new observational clues: a Dyson swarm would show an unusually "clean" spectrum—lacking the silicate dust emissions of ordinary stars—and might produce irregular brightness fluctuations as its components orbit. While no technosignature has been confirmed, this research equips astronomers with a sharper lens to distinguish alien engineering from cosmic mirages. The hunt is on.
why_it_matters: Finding a Dyson swarm would be the first evidence of intelligent life beyond Earth, fundamentally altering our understanding of our place in the universe. Even the act of searching stretches our imagination and pushes telescope technology to its limits, opening up new discoveries along the way.

questions.question: What is a Dyson swarm?
options: A collection of orbiting solar panels around a star
A cloud of insects that swarm around streetlights
A cluster of black holes in the galaxy
A solid shell completely enclosing a star
questions.correct_answer: A collection of orbiting solar panels around a star

questions.question: What would a Dyson swarm do to a star's appearance on the H-R diagram?
options: Make it disappear from the diagram entirely
Move it to the upper left corner
Increase its visible brightness dramatically
Greatly lower its effective temperature while keeping total energy output the same
questions.correct_answer: Greatly lower its effective temperature while keeping total energy output the same

They are the brightest stars in the sky

background_read: The search for alien technology stretches back decades. In 1960, physicist Freeman Dyson suggested that a truly advanced civilization might build an enormous structure around its star to harvest energy. This concept later became linked to the Kardashev scale, which ranks civilizations by how much energy they can use.

While a solid sphere is physically impossible, modern ideas favor a Dyson swarm—millions of orbiting solar collectors that form a cloud around the star. Such a structure would change the star's light into heat, making it look cold and dark to optical telescopes but bright in infrared.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST—the most powerful space telescope, launched in 2021) can detect exactly that infrared glow. Projects like Hephaistos (named after the Greek god of fire and metalworking) use data from the Gaia spacecraft and other surveys to hunt for stars that appear unnaturally cold.

So far, a handful of candidates have been found, but none confirmed. Astronomers are now refining the telltale signs that would separate a genuine alien power plant from a natural, dusty young star. This study gives them a sharp new tool for that task.

perspectives.description: If Dyson swarms exist, they prove that civilizations can survive their technological youth and harness incredible amounts of energy. This would offer hope that humanity could one day do the same and that intelligent life is common in the galaxy.

Every mysterious signal so far has turned out to be natural—pulsars, quasars, or dusty stars. Jumping to an alien explanation without exhaustively ruling out all natural causes risks creating false hope and can sidetrack science from more mundane but important work.

The study is valuable even if no technosignature is found. By modeling what a Dyson swarm would look like, researchers define a new search space and learn more about how stars behave at extreme temperatures, pushing stellar astrophysics forward regardless of the outcome.

Next-generation surveys with JWST and the upcoming Vera Rubin Observatory will scan billions of objects. A single solid detection could reframe astronomy’s goals overnight. Preparations should include international protocols for verifying and announcing such a discovery to avoid confusion and ensure global cooperation.
